"Obliquely" means not directly — either in a physical direction (not in a straight line, but at an angle) or in the way something is said or done (not plainly, but through hints, suggestions, or a roundabout approach).

Think of it as the opposite of going straight at something — whether that "something" is a physical direction or a point you're trying to make.

1. Physical / Literal Sense — At a slant or angle

When something moves, falls, is positioned, or happens at an angle rather than straight on, it happens obliquely.

"The afternoon sun shone obliquely through the blinds, casting long diagonal shadows across the floor."

Here, the sunlight isn't falling straight down or hitting the floor head-on — it's coming in at a slant.

"She was standing obliquely to the door, half-turned away."

She isn't facing the door directly — her body is angled.

This sense is common in technical fields — optics (light hitting a surface obliquely), anatomy (muscles running obliquely across the body), and geometry (a line cutting obliquely through another line at a non-right angle).

2. Figurative / Communicative Sense — Indirectly, without saying it plainly

This is the far more common use in everyday English. When someone says or does something obliquely, they are deliberately avoiding directness — hinting, suggesting, or implying something rather than stating it outright.

"She obliquely suggested that he wasn't qualified for the job."

She didn't say "You're not qualified." She hinted at it — maybe by emphasizing the experience the role requires, or by mentioning someone else's strong credentials. The message got through, but it wasn't stated openly.

"He obliquely criticized the government's policy in his speech."

He didn't attack it head-on. He spoke around it — through analogies, comparisons, or carefully chosen words that make his disapproval clear to a listening ear without him ever saying "this policy is wrong."
Why Do People Speak or Act Obliquely?

This is where it gets interesting. Someone acts obliquely for one of a few reasons:

1. To be polite or tactful. Directly saying "Your work is poor" feels harsh. Saying obliquely, "I wonder if the approach could be refined a little," softens the message while still communicating it.

2. To protect themselves. If you criticize something directly, you own that criticism fully. Speaking obliquely gives you plausible deniability — "I didn't say that, I only implied..."

3. To test the waters. Before committing to a position, people sometimes raise an idea obliquely to see how others react — without putting themselves fully on the line.

4. To be subtle or sophisticated. In literature, politics, or intellectual discourse, oblique references can be a sign of nuance — a preference for suggestion over bluntness.
The Key Feeling of the Word

When you encounter obliquely, ask yourself: "Is something going at an angle — physically or communicatively?"

  • A slanted beam of light → oblique direction
  • A veiled criticism that never names its target → oblique communication

The underlying flavour is always the same: something is coming at you sideways, not straight on.

• Oblique ≠ vague. Something vague is unclear or fuzzy. Something oblique can be very pointed and clear in its meaning — it just reaches you through an indirect route. A well-placed oblique remark can sting just as much as a direct one; you just can't quote it back as easily.
  • Oblique ≠ dishonest. Speaking obliquely isn't the same as lying. The information is present — it just isn't handed to you on a plate. You have to read between the lines.
  • It often implies intent. When someone does something obliquely, there's usually a reason they chose not to be direct. The word quietly implies awareness and choice, not accident.

Words that mean something similar:

  • Indirectly
  • In a roundabout way
  • Allusively (by allusion)
  • Sideways (in physical contexts)
  • Diagonally (in physical/spatial contexts)

Words that are the opposite:

  • Directly
  • Straightforwardly
  • Bluntly
  • Head-on
  • Squarely
A Few More Examples to Cement It

"The journalist obliquely accused the minister of corruption without ever using that word."

"Light entering a pool of water obliquely bends as it crosses into the denser medium."

"Rather than asking outright, she obliquely brought up how expensive city apartments had become — her real question being whether he could afford the rent."

"He glanced at her obliquely, not wanting her to catch him looking."
"Obliquely" means at an angle — whether that angle is physical (a slanting direction) or figurative (an indirect, roundabout way of saying or doing something).
